title: Animals' rights
hook: don't overload, don't brand faces, don't make them targets (Muslim)

segments.voice: Yesterday, 'aqd, the contract, and your line: clear terms. Clear words, a free yes, and no gamble hidden inside.

Tears, running from a camel's eyes. That's where a report in Abu Dawud begins, in a walled garden in Medina belonging to a man of the Ansar. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ steps inside, and the camel tied there sees him and begins to groan. He strokes it behind the ears until it settles, then asks: whose camel is this? A young man comes running. And the Prophet tells him to fear God about this animal, because it has complained that its owner starves it and wears it out.
screen: `A CAMEL IN A WALLED GARDEN.` → `IT GROANS, THEN SETTLES.` → `IT COMPLAINED OF YOU.`

segments.voice: Day two hundred seventy-two gave us the man who carried water up a well for a thirsty dog. Today, the law's side. The Qur'an sets the frame. In surah six, every creature on the earth and every bird that flies on two wings are communities like you, and they too will be gathered to their Lord. Communities, not furniture. From that the fiqh books draw duties, and today's three come from the hadith. First, don't overload. Another report in Abu Dawud tells of the Prophet passing a camel so thin its back had nearly reached its belly: fear God about these animals that cannot speak; ride them while they are fit, and eat of them while they are fit. The jurists made it a rule: an owner must feed an animal and may not work it beyond its strength. Second, don't brand or strike faces. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet forbids hitting the face and branding the face, and when he passes a donkey branded on its face, he curses whoever did it. Third, don't make them targets. Also in Sahih Muslim, Ibn Umar comes across young men shooting at a bird they've tied up. They scatter, and he tells them the Prophet cursed anyone who makes a living thing a target. So the fiqh books speak of an animal's rights the way they speak of a neighbor's: food, rest, a fair load, a face left unbranded. A camel can't file a complaint. The tradition says it filed one anyway, and the Prophet heard it.
screen: `COMMUNITIES LIKE YOU.` · `DON'T OVERLOAD: FEED AND REST THEM.` · `DON'T BRAND OR STRIKE THE FACE.` · `DON'T MAKE THEM TARGETS.`

segments.voice: If there's a pet near you, check its water and sit with it a while. If not, bring to mind an animal you see often, a neighbor's dog, a bird on the wire, and ask what it needs that only a person can give: food, water, shade, a lighter load. Hold it kindly, and if you pray, you can remember it there.
Animals' rights. In Islamic law, what an animal is owed: food, rest, a fair load, a face left unharmed, and never to be used as a target. Today's word.
Your line: they have rights. Even the ones who can't speak for themselves. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: Islamic law requires owners to feed and rest their animals and not to overwork them, and forbids striking or branding their faces and using living creatures as targets.

chat.says: Does Islam say anything about how we treat animals?
options: Yes. Feed them, don't overwork them, and never brand their faces or use them as targets.
Only about which animals are halal to eat; the rest is up to the owner.
Not really. Animals aren't communities, so they have no rights at all.
chat.meaning: The Qur'an calls animals communities like you, and the hadith forbid starving or overloading them, branding faces and shooting at living targets.

Ansar.meaning: the Prophet's helpers among the people of Medina

Abu Dawud.meaning: compiler of a well-known hadith collection

Ibn Umar.meaning: a companion of the Prophet, son of Umar

notes: 6:38 paraphrased (Pickthall: 'peoples like unto you'); 'gathered to their Lord' paraphrases the end of the verse. Confirm.
Abu Dawud 2549: confirm details (tears, stroking behind the ears, the young Ansari owner, 'starves it and wears it out').
Abu Dawud 2548: confirm wording paraphrase and number (Sahl ibn al-Hanzaliyyah).
Muslim 2116–2117 and 1958: confirm numbers; some versions say a hen rather than a bird.
Jurists' rules on feeding and not overworking: confirm general framing (some schools allow a judge to compel an owner).
'The face, it seems, is protected even on a donkey' is the narrator's observation.
